source.title: Hierarchical Frequency Tagging Probe (HFTP): A Unified Approach to Investigate Syntactic Structure Representations in Large Language Models and the Human Brain
source.authors: Jingmin An; Yilong Song; Ruolin Yang; Nai Ding; Lingxi Lu; Yuxuan Wang; Wei Wang; Chu Zhuang; Qian Wang; Fang Fang

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures syntactic representational alignment between language models and the human brain, not convergence between independently trained models, vision-language alignment, seed convergence, or feature recurrence as specified by the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports model-to-brain similarity values, which are related to representational alignment but do not measure the convergence named by any claim version. Its frequency-tagging results and neuron counts are not rows because they do not measure that convergence. The model-to-brain global scores are recorded under versions ["none"].
record.test_reason: The study measures similarity between LLM syntactic representations and human sEEG responses, using RSA and predictive encoding. It never compares independently trained models with each other, vision with language models, seeds, cross-model maps or matched features. Every version names model-to-model convergence, so none is tested. The Hosseini et al. brain–model universality work is only cited in related work.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is essentially correct. Add two points: the authors also conclude that LLMs integrate sentence and phrase processing within the same layers, whereas the brain segregates them across regions. They also raise the question of whether model improvements come from human-like mechanisms.
record.recipe_differences: Uses HFTP frequency-domain probes and model-to-brain SRDM-RSA, with a predictive-encoding analysis; it does not use a method testing the original model-to-model convergence claim.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports SRDM-RSA and predictive-encoding analyses, and sentence and phrase corpora. It says phrase-corpus differences between upgraded model pairs are compressed in predictive encoding; Llama 3.1 is slightly above Llama 2 there, unlike the sentence-corpus result.

fits_no_version.finding: Model-to-brain syntactic similarity is higher for the left hemisphere in every model, corpus and method. Upgraded models diverge: Gemma 2 is above Gemma, and Llama 3.1 is below Llama 2 (0.514 vs 0.645, left, sentence RSA). The ordering compresses or flips under predictive encoding on the phrase corpus.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: LLM–brain syntactic alignment does not rise steadily with model capability or version, and its ordering depends on the alignment method and corpus.

fits_no_version.finding: All six LLMs contain sentence- and phrase-selective MLP neurons. Their counts covary strongly across layers (r 0.754 to 0.994), but the layer locations differ by model family: early in Gemma, middle in GPT-2, late in Llama and GLM.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Syntax-tuned neuron types recur across LLM families, though at different depths. This is not a test of shared individual features.

record.peer_reviewed: 39th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2025)
record.problems: The authors state that only a small set of model architectures and parameter scales was evaluated. Brain data were from Chinese sEEG participants; the English brain analysis is preliminary and from one participant. Global table scores are reported without uncertainty estimates, although the paper reports ANOVA statistics and p-values for model differences.
record.rows_left_out: The ROI-specific model-to-brain values in Tables 1–4 are not separately rowed: the tables contain many additional region-by-model-by-hemisphere results, and the 48 global scores were prioritized to retain all models, corpora, hemispheres, and both alignment methods. The paper's frequency-tagging neuron/channel counts and naturalistic-corpus spectral patterns were also left out because they do not measure model-to-model convergence or model-to-brain alignment.

untested.parts: No model-to-model alignment is measured, so convergence with scale is untested. Model-to-brain scores across six models of differing scale are adjacent evidence only.
No vision models or image–caption pairs.
No runs of the same architecture from different seeds.
No mapping, stitching or relative-representation transfer between models. The ridge regression maps models to the brain, not to other models.
Syntax-selective MLP neurons are found in all six models, but neurons are not matched or compared across models. Whether the same features recur is untested.
Method dependence (RSA vs predictive encoding, sentence vs phrase corpus) is shown only for model-to-brain scores, not for model-to-model convergence.
Training-data explanations are offered for model-to-brain differences, not for model-to-model convergence.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T6/discusses classification and its all-'none' row links are correct. Row values were spot-checked against Tables 1–4 and match. No verdicts are given because no version is tested.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test whether independently trained models become more aligned as model size or capability increases.
No vision-language model pairs or paired image-caption representations are tested.
No comparison across random initialization seeds of the same architecture is reported.
The study uses representational similarity analysis but does not test mapping, stitching, relative representations, or unpaired interchangeability between models.
It does not test recurrence of interpretable features or circuits across models.
Although it reports model-to-brain alignment with two methods and multiple corpora, it does not test whether measured convergence between models depends on metric, settings, or inputs.
The paper discusses model-to-brain alignment and possible training-data explanations, but does not test partial convergence between models or its causes.
